newsitem.title: UK: UK Tories risk losing touch with voters-Howe.
newsitem.headline: UK Tories risk losing touch with voters-Howe.

text.p: Britain's defeated Conservative party risks further alienating voters if it veers to the right by choosing William Hague or John Redwood as its next leader, former deputy prime minister Lord Geoffrey Howe said on Monday.

Hague and Redwood are contesting the leadership on a platform of hostility to the European Union's single currency, whereas voters signalled by electing Labour on May 1 that they wanted a more balanced view of Europe, Howe told BBC radio.
He said only former finance minister Kenneth Clarke, the third candidate in Tuesday's second leadership ballot, could reflect that balanced view and hold the party together.

"What I'm more concerned about is that if we're led either by William Hague or John Redwood, there will open up an even wider gap between the Conservative party and the great mass of public opinion, business opinion..." Howe said.

By focusing obsessively on the single currency, the Conservatives risked repeating the mistake of the Labour party of the early 1980s, which made itself unelectable by indulging in a purely doctrinal debate over nuclear disarmament, he said.
"The Tory party risks drifting away from the people.

"If it is to get back in touch with the people whose votes we need, then we need to return to the centre ground and that is surely the cataclysmic lesson of the election we've just lost so catastrophically," Howe said.
He said it would be a reckless waste of Clarke's experience if he were rejected in Tuesday's ballot.
Howe was broadly echoing another former deputy prime minister, Michael Heseltine, who said on Sunday that the party might collapse without Clarke to hold it together.
"There is no way in which we will win a general election unless we remember that we have always done that, appealing to a wide constituency across the United Kingdom," he said.

Clarke himself underlined the risk of the Conservatives heading into an ideological ghetto under Redwood or Hague, saying few pro-Europeans would be willing to serve under them if they based their appeal on hard-line Euro-scepticism.

The three contenders will answer questions from their colleagues later on Monday, while Redwood is to hold a concluding press conference at which he will promise to unite the party by providing strong leadership and renegotiating Britain's relations with Europe.
"If the European question remains unanswered, two teams will remain on the Tory turf kicking the ball and each other."
"If there was a magic fudge which could hold the party together, John Major would have found it by now," he said in a statement.
